one_liner: Faster recovery: median {{n:rec_rdv}} with remdesivir vs {{n:rec_pbo}} with placebo (rate ratio for recovery {{n:rr_rec}}).
one_liner_plain: Remdesivir shortened time to recovery in hospitalized Covid-19

citation.title: Remdesivir for the Treatment of Covid-19 — Final Report
citation.authors: Beigel JH, Tomashek KM, Dodd LE, et al.

sections.background: Early in the pandemic, several drugs had been tried against Covid-19, but no antiviral had been shown to work. Remdesivir, an inhibitor of the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, was an early candidate because it inhibits SARS-CoV-2 in vitro. ACTT-1 was the NIH-sponsored, double-blind, placebo-controlled test of whether it actually helped hospitalized patients. This page covers the final report.

methods.design: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at 60 trial sites and 13 subsites in the United States, Europe, and Asia; randomization stratified by site and disease severity.
methods.population: Adults hospitalized with Covid-19 and evidence of lower respiratory tract infection. {{n:n_total}} underwent randomization ({{n:n_rdv}} to remdesivir, {{n:n_pbo}} to placebo).
methods.intervention: Intravenous remdesivir: 200 mg loading dose on day 1, then 100 mg daily for up to 9 more days.
methods.comparator: Matching placebo for up to 10 days. Both groups received standard supportive care.
methods.primary_endpoint: Time to recovery: the first day, within 28 days after enrollment, in category 1, 2, or 3 of the eight-category ordinal scale (discharged, or hospitalized only for infection-control or other nonmedical reasons).
methods.follow-up: Daily assessment through day 29. The primary outcome was originally day-15 clinical status and was changed to time to recovery in response to outside evidence that Covid-19 can run a longer course.

sections.results: Remdesivir shortened recovery: a median of {{n:rec_rdv}} versus {{n:rec_pbo}} with placebo (rate ratio for recovery {{n:rr_rec}}; 95% CI 1.12 to 1.49; P<0.001). Patients on remdesivir were also more likely to be better on the ordinal scale at day 15 (odds ratio {{n:or15}}). The benefit was clearest in patients on low-flow oxygen (ordinal score 5; rate ratio {{n:rr_os5}}). Confidence intervals were wide for patients not on oxygen, on high-flow oxygen, or on mechanical ventilation or ECMO, where the rate ratio was {{n:rr_os7}}. Kaplan-Meier mortality by day 29 was {{n:m29_rdv}} with remdesivir versus {{n:m29_pbo}} with placebo (hazard ratio {{n:hr29}}; 95% CI 0.52 to 1.03), a difference that was not statistically significant. Serious adverse events were less common with remdesivir ({{n:sae_rdv}} vs {{n:sae_pbo}}), and the initial hospital stay was shorter (median {{n:stay_rdv}} vs {{n:stay_pbo}}).
sections.conclusions: Remdesivir was superior to placebo in shortening the time to recovery in adults hospitalized with Covid-19 and lower respiratory tract infection. The authors suggest it may also have prevented progression to more severe respiratory disease and reduced the use of scarce hospital resources.
sections.limitations: The mortality difference did not reach statistical significance. Subgroup estimates outside the low-flow oxygen group had wide confidence intervals, and the median recovery time for ventilated patients could not be estimated, suggesting follow-up was too short for that group. A normal saline placebo was used at some sites because matching placebo ran short, with the infusions masked to keep the blind.
sections.practice_impact: ACTT-1 was the first double-blind trial to show that an antiviral helps hospitalized Covid-19 patients. Remdesivir became a standard option for inpatients, especially those on low-flow oxygen, and the benefit persisted after adjusting for steroid use, suggesting it may add to dexamethasone.

numbers.label: Trial sites

numbers.label: Median time to recovery, remdesivir
numbers.source_quote: Those who received remdesivir had a median recovery time of 10 days (95% confidence interval [CI], 9 to 11), as compared with 15 days (95% CI, 13 to 18) among those who received placebo (rate ratio for recovery, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.12 to 1.49; P<0.001, by a log-rank test).

hero_findings.headline: Median time to recovery with remdesivir (placebo: 15 days); rate ratio 1.29
Rate ratio for recovery in patients on low-flow oxygen, the clearest benefit
Mortality by day 29 with remdesivir (placebo: 15.2%); hazard ratio 0.73, not significant
Median initial hospital stay with remdesivir (placebo: 17 days)

must_include_map.excerpt: Those who received remdesivir had a median recovery time of 10 days (95% confidence interval [CI], 9 to 11), as compared with 15 days (95% CI, 13 to 18) among those who received placebo (rate ratio for recovery, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.12 to 1.49; P<0.001, by a log-rank test).

Kaplan-Meier estimates of mortality by day 15 were 6.7% in the remdesivir group and 11.9% in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.36 to 0.83); the estimates by day 29 were 11.4% and 15.2% in two groups, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.52 to 1.03).
Our data show that remdesivir was superior to placebo in shortening the time to recovery in adults who were hospitalized with Covid-19 and had evidence of lower respiratory tract infection.
